awd_abstract_narration:
The 2025 Midwest Numerical Analysis Day (MWNADay) is scheduled to take place on April 5-6, 2025, at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. This conference will provide a collaborative platform for researchers from the Midwest region and beyond to share knowledge and build connections in numerical analysis, computational mathematics, and related applied fields. By fostering a welcoming and low-pressure environment, MWNADay has become particularly valuable for early-career researchers, enabling them to present their work, exchange ideas, and explore collaborations. This event will also emphasize and encourage participation from individuals across many types of groups and institutions with limited access to major conferences. As computational technologies continue to impact various disciplines, MWNADay serves a crucial role in strengthening the community and advancing the frontiers of computational and numerical sciences.

MWNADay 2025 focuses on promoting advancements in numerical analysis and scientific computing by providing a forum for researchers to discuss cutting-edge developments, exchange methodologies, and explore interdisciplinary applications. The conference will draw participants from various academic and research institutions, including (according to the Carnegie Classification System) the 26 R1 (very high research activity) and 32 R2 (high research activity) universities in the Midwest, to share insights and engage in collaborative discussions. Central to its mission is the development of efficient numerical algorithms and their theoretical foundations, which are essential for addressing challenges in fields such as fluid dynamics, biomechanics, and geophysics. The local organizing committee aims to facilitate the participation of a broad audience, particularly early-career researchers, as well as faculty from institutions where access to major research conferences may be limited. MWNADay will offer a range of activities, including technical presentations, poster sessions, and networking opportunities, to inspire innovation and foster partnerships among attendees. Additionally, the conference aims to bridge gaps between research communities by integrating junior and senior researchers and advancing knowledge transfer across disciplines, ultimately contributing to the broader fields of numerical analysis and computational mathematics. The conference website is https://math.unl.edu/midwest-numerical-analysis-day-2025

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The Midwest Numerical Analysis Day (MWNADay) 2025, hosted by the University of Nebraska-Lincoln on April 5-6, 2025, successfully brought together researchers, practitioners, and students to advance the fields of numerical analysis and scientific computing. As a regional conference with a legacy dating back to 1990, this event provided a vital forum for exchanging ideas and fostering interdisciplinary collaborations across the Midwest.

Intellectual Merit: The project achieved significant intellectual merit by addressing the evolving challenges of modern computing, which is essential for modeling complex real-world problems in fields such as fluid dynamics, biomechanics, and geosciences.

Key Technical Outcomes: The conference featured four plenary lectures by renowned researchers: Akram Aldroubi (Vanderbilt University), Jing-Mei Qiu (University of Delaware), Beatrice Riviere (Rice University), and Dongbin Xiu (The Ohio State University). Presentations covered high-impact areas including high-order numerical methods, data-driven modeling for "Digital Twins," neural network-based machine learning for PDEs, and structure-preserving algorithms. Through 35 specialized minisymposium talks, 9 contributed talks, and 9 poster presentations, participants explored advanced algorithms for fluid-structure interactions, nonlocal models, and discontinuous Galerkin methods. A dedicated panel discussion shifted the focus from specific results to research methodology, helping junior investigators understand how experts choose mathematical approaches and envision the future of the field. The panel included diverse perspectives from: Ken Bloom (University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Physics), Brittany Duncan (University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Computing), Michael Parks (Oak Ridge National Laboratory), Beatrice Riviere (Rice University), Yanzhi Zhang (Missouri University of Science and Technology)

Broader Impacts: The project’s broader impacts centered on professional development and community building, particularly for early-career researchers. The conference provided an affordable, low-pressure environment for graduate students and postdocs to present their research and enhance communication skills. Approximately 70% of participants typically represent junior researchers; the NSF grant specifically funded travel and lodging for over 40 out-of-town students, postdocs, and early-career faculty who lacked other financial support. By hosting the event in Lincoln, Nebraska, an EPSCoR state, the project stimulated research activity in the Midwest, reducing the geographical isolation often felt by researchers outside of coastal hubs. The event facilitated direct interaction between mathematicians and scientists from other departments, including Agricultural Engineering, Biology, and Physics, to encourage the application of numerical techniques to diverse scientific challenges.

Over its lifecycle, this award supported the first-ever hosting of MWNADay at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. It successfully engaged faculty and students from R1 and R2 universities across 12 Midwest states, strengthening the regional computational mathematics infrastructure. By combining high-level plenary sessions with student-focused minisymposia, the project ensured that cutting-edge theoretical advances were directly shared with the next generation of American scientists.
